title: Peptide Vial Label Revisions: Keep Old and New Rolls Apart
seoTitle: Peptide Vial Label Artwork Changeover | RP Labels
description: A practical changeover checklist for custom peptide vial labels: approved artwork version, roll identity, old stock, line clearance and a first labeled vial.
alt: AI-generated fully printed RP Research V1 and V2 sample-label rolls separated on a bench beside a labeled glass vial
caption: AI-generated changeover illustration, not an RP production record. Vial names, version marks and roll identifiers are fictional examples.
intro: A corrected file is not enough if yesterday's roll is still sitting next to today's vial line.
sources: FDA: packaging and label change-management inspection concepts for biologic products
FDA: API GMP guidance on removing prior labeling materials before use

title: Peptide Vial Label Height: Leave the Cap, Shoulder and Viewing Area Clear
seoTitle: Peptide Vial Label Height and Cap Clearance | RP
description: Measure usable straight-wall glass, crimp-cap clearance and viewing space before approving the height of custom peptide vial labels.
alt: AI-generated printed RP Research label on a small glass vial beneath its shoulder with a caliper and flat label proof
caption: AI-generated vial-size example, not a measured RP fit test or a validated fill-level marking. Batch and code details are illustrative.
intro: The vial can measure tall enough on paper while the printable straight wall is much shorter.
sources: HERMA: vial wrap-around labeling and precise positioning
HERMA: labels on small cylindrical containers
GS1: barcode considerations on curved surfaces

title: Supplement Bottle Front Panels: Reserve Identity and Net Quantity First
seoTitle: Supplement Label Front Panel Layout | RP Labels
description: Plan custom supplement label artwork around the front-panel statement of identity and net quantity before logos, finishes and decorative claims take the space.
alt: AI-generated botanical RP Wellness supplement bottle and flat proof showing front identity and lower net quantity placement
caption: AI-generated artwork example, not a compliant approved supplement label. The brand and its regulatory reviewer must approve the final copy and layout.
intro: A strong logo gets the first glance. It must not push the product identity or quantity out of the usable front panel.
sources: FDA: general dietary supplement label statements and principal display panel
FDA: statement of identity on supplement packaging
FDA: net quantity placement and measurement

title: Supplement Label Barcodes: Do Flavor and Count Variants Need Separate GTINs?
seoTitle: Supplement SKU GTIN and Barcode Planning | RP
description: Create a supplement label SKU and barcode matrix before printing new flavors or bottle counts; keep brand-owned GTIN assignment separate from barcode artwork.
alt: AI-generated RP Wellness citrus and berry supplement bottles with distinct sample barcodes and a two-row SKU planning sheet
caption: AI-generated SKU-planning illustration. Barcode-like marks and DEMO numbers are not valid assigned GS1 identifiers or scan-tested symbols.
intro: Two flavors can share a design system. They should not inherit the same retail identity by accident.
sources: GS1: new product versus change, including added flavor
GS1: declared net content change rule
GS1: how many GTINs are needed for variants

title: Hologram Seals on Curved Bottle Caps: Test the Fold Before Ordering
seoTitle: Hologram Seal on Curved Bottle Cap | RP Labels
description: Compare flexible holographic seal samples across the cap rim and curved bottle shoulder, checking edge lift, opening path and visible removal evidence.
alt: AI-generated original RP Secure holographic strips across curved jar cap rims showing flush and lifting-edge examples
caption: AI-generated geometry comparison. Neither pictured seal is evidence of tested RP adhesive strength, tamper resistance or authentication performance.
intro: A flat hologram swatch says little about a seal that must cross a cap rim and then hold onto a curved bottle wall.
sources: HERMA: curved-surface label conformability and small diameters
Avery Dennison: facestock flexibility for complex package shapes
